claims.text: High configurational entropy induces severe local lattice distortions in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Severe lattice distortions impede dislocation motion and thereby enhance mechanical strength.
Lattice distortions catalyze uniform formation of an adherent, Al-rich or other lightweight-element-rich protective oxide layer.

The proposed combination of lattice distortion and protective-oxide formation explains the simultaneous low density, strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance of lightweight HEAs.
The initial as-cast alloy has a single-phase or dual-phase microstructure with nanoscale lattice distortions.
Reducing the number of principal elements while retaining similar overall chemistry suppresses lattice-distortion effects.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates or oxide-nucleation sites promote formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide film.
High configurational entropy produces pronounced lattice strain and dislocation pinning.
The proposed structural features favor rapid and uniform oxidation of Al or similarly active lightweight elements.
The resulting protective oxide film resists high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
The HEA will have higher yield strength than the lower-entropy baseline.
The HEA will have lower corrosion rates than the lower-entropy baseline.
The HEA will have lower oxidation rates than the lower-entropy baseline.
The HEA will exhibit greater lattice distortion than the lower-entropy baseline.
The HEA will form a more uniform and adherent protective oxide film than the lower-entropy baseline.
The mechanism should cease to hold when lightweight oxide-forming elements such as Al or Ti are absent.
At sufficiently extreme exposure temperatures, deterioration or spallation of the protective oxide film eliminates its effectiveness.
